title: Finding the Way
intro: Birds, turtles and even butterflies travel thousands of kilometres to places they have never seen. How do they know where to go?

passage: Every year, billions of animals make long journeys across land, sea and sky. Birds fly between continents, whales cross entire oceans and insects travel thousands of kilometres to places they have never seen before. Many of these journeys are repeated every year for the whole of an animal's life. For centuries, people have wondered how these animals find their way without maps, road signs or the satellite navigation that most of us now rely on. Thanks to new tracking technology, scientists are finally beginning to find some answers, although many mysteries remain.

The distances involved can be astonishing. Small electronic devices attached to Arctic terns, birds that weigh only about a hundred grams, have shown that some of them fly more than 70,000 kilometres a year, travelling from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back again. Over a lifetime of thirty years, a single tern may cover a distance equal to several journeys to the Moon and back. Another bird, the bar-tailed godwit, has been recorded flying from Alaska to New Zealand – more than 11,000 kilometres – without stopping once to eat, drink or rest.

One of the simplest navigation tools is the sun. Because the sun moves across the sky during the day, an animal can only use it as a compass if it also knows what time it is. Experiments have shown that many birds and insects have an internal clock that allows them to adjust for the sun's movement. Monarch butterflies, which fly up to 4,000 kilometres from Canada and the northern United States to forests in central Mexico, rely heavily on this kind of sun compass. Remarkably, none of the butterflies that make this journey has ever made it before.

The sun, however, is not always visible, and many animals travel at night or under cloudy skies. For these journeys, the Earth's magnetic field appears to play a vital role. The strength and angle of the magnetic field vary slightly from place to place, so in theory an animal that can sense it has access to a kind of invisible map. Young sea turtles seem to remember the magnetic 'signature' of the beach where they hatched, and many females return to the same area to lay their own eggs years later, after travelling thousands of kilometres across the ocean.

Exactly how animals detect the magnetic field is still one of the great puzzles of biology. One theory suggests that birds have special proteins in their eyes that react to magnetism, which might allow them to 'see' the field as a pattern of light and shade. Another suggests that tiny particles of iron in some animals' bodies act like the needle of a compass. It is possible that different species use different methods, or even a combination of several.

Many animals also use their other senses. Homing pigeons, which can return to their lofts from hundreds of kilometres away, appear to combine information from the sun and the magnetic field with familiar landmarks such as rivers, roads and coastlines. Some experiments suggest that smell may help too: pigeons that could not smell had more difficulty finding their way home. Salmon, meanwhile, are thought to use smell to recognise the river where they were born when they return to it to breed. Even honeybees use landmarks, together with the position of the sun, to find their way between flowers and the hive.

Understanding animal navigation is not only a matter of scientific curiosity. Bright city lights can confuse birds that migrate at night, and some researchers are concerned that electrical equipment may interfere with animals' magnetic sense. Knowing which routes animals use, and where they stop to rest and feed, also helps governments to decide which areas most need protection. As one researcher put it, if we want these extraordinary journeys to continue, we first need to understand them.
